activity_context.topic_title: Finding the Area of a Polar Region

examples.knowledge_point: Finding the Area Bounded by the Loop of a Limaçon
examples.problem:
Find the area bounded by the polar curve $r = 1+2\cos\theta$ for $\dfrac{2\pi}{3} \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{4\pi}{3},$ as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14060520/assets/6bfa0990b560bcb09f2a9eb0b9542296f2a8f1c196b6740702e81c59941d66c5.png)
examples.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A = \dfrac{1}{2} \int_{\theta_1}^{\theta_2} r^2(\theta) \, \textrm{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta) = 1+2\cos(\theta),$ $\theta_1=\dfrac{2\pi}{3},$ and $\theta_2=\dfrac{4\pi}{3},$ this gives 

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}(1+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(\theta ))^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}(1+4\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta +4{cos}^{2}⁡\theta )\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+4\cdot \frac{1}{2}{\int }_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta ) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+2\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(3\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+4\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}+\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{2\pi /3}^{4\pi /3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\pi -4\sqrt{3}+\sqrt{3}) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}(2\pi -3\sqrt{3}).\end{aligned}
$$

feedback.worked_solution:
The area bounded by a polar curve is given by

$$
A=\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}(\theta )\text{d}\theta \,.
$$

When $r(\theta )=3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $, ${\theta }_{1}=-\frac{\pi }{4}$ and ${\theta }_{2}=\frac{\pi }{4}$, this gives

$$
\begin{aligned}A & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}{r}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta )^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta \,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{2}\cdot \frac{1}{2}{\int }_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}(1+\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\theta ))\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{9}{4}\theta \,{|}_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4}+\frac{9}{8}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\theta )\,{|}_{-\pi /4}^{\pi /4} \\  & =\frac{9}{4}(\frac{\pi }{4}-(-\frac{\pi }{4}))+\frac{9}{8}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{2})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(-\frac{\pi }{2})) \\  & =\frac{9}{4}(\frac{\pi }{2})+\frac{9}{8}(1+1) \\  & =\frac{9\pi }{8}+\frac{9}{4} \\  & =\frac{9\pi +18}{8}.\end{aligned}
$$
